newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: SYDNEY OLYMPICS PRIME TARGET FOR CREDIT CARD FRAUD.
newsitem.headline: SYDNEY OLYMPICS PRIME TARGET FOR CREDIT CARD FRAUD.

text.p: The Sydney 2000 Olympic Games will be a prime target for credit card fraud, drawing criminals from around the world to prey on foreign tourists and local businesses, an Australian report warned on Wednesday.
The Australian Institute of Criminology paper said Australia to date has largely been spared from international credit card fraud, which is now a billion-dollar worldwide industry.
"Strategic planning...should be carried out now if the vulnerabilities of the 2000 Olympic Games are to be avoided," stressed the report by institute analyst Russell Smith.
"When Sydney hosts the Olympic Games in September 2000, there will be hundreds of thousands of visitors coming to Australia," Smith said.
"Amongst them will be some who may seek to perpetrate plastic card fraud and others who, unfortunately, will be victims of such fraud."
The report cited fake Visa "Olympia" cards bearing the Visa symbol and the five Olympic rings that circulated at the 1992 Barcelona Games. Visa never actually produced such cards.
Australia losses an estimated A$6.0 million (US$4.2 million) a year from credit card fraud, compared with worldwide losses of up to A$2.0 billion, the report said.
But the report warned that a range of factors would combine at the Sydney Olympics to offer rich pickings to fraudsters using stolen or fake credit cards or stored-value cards.

It said local traders will be unfamiliar with the scores of different plastic cards foreign visitors will bring, while some tourists could be conned because of their lack of English and unfamiliarity with local transaction systems.
"Policy-makers should recognise that the plastic card industry is being deliberately targeted by organised criminal enterprises from around the globe," Smith warned.
"The perception that it is only an industry problem is no longer sustainable."
Smith urged increased cooperation and information sharing among law enforcement agencies, traders and financial institutions around the world.
